b: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. Our guest, Jorma Kaukonen, was the lead guitar player and a founding member of Jefferson Airplane, one of the bands that defined psychedelic rock of the 1960s and served as the soundtrack for San Francisco's Summer of Love. Jorma's also had a long career with his other very popular band, Hot Tuna, which he still tours with. He spoke with FRESH AIR's executive producer, Sam Briger, about his life and career. Here's Sam.

SAM BRIGER, BYLINE: If you've ever heard the song "Somebody To Love" or "White Rabbit" by Jefferson Airplane, you've heard Jorma Kaukonen play electric guitar. But Jorma's one of those rare musicians with a compelling style on both acoustic and electric guitars. He's known as a terrific fingerstyle guitarist, deeply influenced by the music of Reverend Gary Davis, a blues and gospel musician who had a resurgence during the 1960s folk scene. Jorma was a Bay Area folky back then, meeting other like-minded musicians who would go on to acclaim as rock and roll phenoms - Jerry Garcia, his soon-to-be band member Paul Kantner and Janis Joplin - who he would accompany at local hootenannies.

Jorma left Jefferson Airplane in the early '70s to concentrate on his other band, Hot Tuna, and other solo projects. His 1974 album "Quah" is one of my favorite albums. He wrote a great memoir published in 2018 called "Been So Long," which details his tumultuous family upbringing, his life as a rock star and recovery from alcohol and drug addictions. At 85, he's still on the road playing gigs with Hot Tuna and as a solo act.

His most recent release is an archival live recording called "Wabash Avenue" from 1965, shortly before he co-founded Jefferson Airplane. One of the tracks on it is an early version of his song "Embryonic Journey," an acoustic instrumental, which would find its way onto Jefferson Airplane's second and most influential album, "Surrealistic Pillow." Let's listen.
BRIGER: That was "Embryonic Journey" from the album "Wabash Avenue" that was released last year from my guest, Jorma Kaukonen. Jorma Kaukonen, welcome to FRESH AIR.
JORMA KAUKONEN: Hey, man. Thanks for having me.
BRIGER: So that was the first song you ever wrote?

KAUKONEN: Yeah. And I'm going to say it's sort of - it's a little self-inflating to say that I wrote that song, but it is the first song that I was - that I ever created, and it was one of those things that happened because, gosh, we had - this folky named Roger Perkins came through San Jose, where I was living at the time. And he played at The Offstage, where we all played back in those days. And he was the first person that I ever saw play in drop D, and he showed it to me, and I went, wow. And I went back to my little house in Santa Clara and started messing around with it. And my roommate at the time said, you know, that sounds like a song. Maybe you should do something with it. And ultimately, "Embryonic Journey" came out of it.
BRIGER: Right. When you say drop D, that means a particular kind of tuning, or you're changing the tuning on a guitar a little bit.
KAUKONEN: (Strumming guitar). I mean, that's a guitar in a straight tuning. (Tuning down, strumming guitar). The six string is down to D when you do that. It makes sort of a sonorous, hypnotic sound.
BRIGER: So that recording that we just heard happened in 1965. Your life was about to change drastically in just a few months, wasn't it?
KAUKONEN: It certainly was. And I remember - you know, Paul Kantner, who was in the Jefferson Airplane also - and he was a San Jose guy, and he had dropped out of Santa Clara.
BRIGER: Which is where you were going to school at the time.

KAUKONEN: Which is where I was going to school at the time. And there was a local music store in San Jose called the Benner Music Company, and Paul was teaching there, and he ultimately got me a job there, too. I mean, so much of that stuff, you know, that mutated into early Jefferson Airplane started at the Benner Music Company on Stevens Creek Boulevard in San Jose.
BRIGER: So you've said that the feeling of a guitar in your lap and your hand on the neck of the guitar has always surrounded you in a protective armor of tranquility. What do you mean by that?
KAUKONEN: Well, first of all, as we're talking here, I'm sitting with a guitar in my lap, even though I may or may not be playing. I mean, I...
BRIGER: I did ask you to bring it. You just didn't bring it as your emotional support guitar.

KAUKONEN: Well, it's my emotional support guitar, yeah. I was sort of a shy kid. And when I - but for some reason, when I started to play the guitar and learned a couple of songs to sing, I wasn't shy at all. And I would imagine that - I mean, I would just play in front of anybody under any circumstances. And to be honest with you, maybe I shouldn't have back then. I don't know, but I did. And so the performing thing, I just never felt uncomfortable with it. And so, once again, with a guitar in my lap and the possibility that I can hide behind playing it was always a great refuge.
BRIGER: Well, let's get back to the first time that you were really struck by the guitar. You had been living in Karachi, Pakistan. Your father had been the director of The Asia Foundation there.
BRIGER: And you had returned back to the States, and were living again in D.C. And you went over to your friend's house, he hadn't seen it in a while, and he had an acoustic guitar.

KAUKONEN: Right. So I had this buddy that - from the neighborhood kind of that I knew. His name was Mike Oliveri. Sad to say he's passed away. But when I came back from Pakistan, Mike had learned to play some bluegrass songs or old-timey - whatever you want to call it - at the time. And I remember going over to his house and going, wow. That's really cool. And so I immediately went back to my dad and I said, I got to have a guitar. And my dad, who was sort of a curmudgeonly fella, said, well, you're going to have to learn to play a couple songs and show me that you're serious about this stuff.

So I got Mike to teach me how to play "Worried Man Blues." And I remember, I borrowed Mike's guitar, and I went back to my dad, and I played "Worried Man Blues." And he said, "Worried Man Blues"? What do you know about being worried? And I thought to myself, well, I'm a teenager, Dad, with a grumpy father. I know a lot about being worried. But I wisely kept that to myself. And ultimately, we went down to the guitar store. It was on Connecticut Avenue. And one of the owners was a great classical player, Sophocles Papas, and I got my first Gibson J-45.
BRIGER: Let's talk a little bit about your family. Your dad, Jorma Sr., his family moved to the States from Finland, and your mom's family, who was Jewish, came from Russia.
BRIGER: And you said you experienced antisemitism growing up, but also, when you were very young, some kids tried to hang you with a coat hanger because your name Jorma...
KAUKONEN: Right. They thought I was a...
BRIGER: ...Sounded like you were a Nazi?

KAUKONEN: Yeah, correct. So my dad was in the Navy in World War II, and at some point - it was before my brother was born, so it had to be before 1945. We were stationed at the Navy language school. It was in Ann Arbor at that time. And my mom came home, and some of the kids from the little housing development where we all lived, again, because I had a weird name, they presumed that I had to be a Nazi spy and (laughter) were starting to string me up. But Mom came through, as she always did.
BRIGER: Jeez. I mean, that's a terrible experience.

KAUKONEN: You know, I'm chuckling about it today as we tell the story. And strangely enough, you'd think it would've been more traumatic for me at the time. But I don't remember it as being traumatic because it's just the way it was back then. And we sort of accepted it. I'm Jorma Jr. My dad's name was Jorma also. But because it upset his buddies in the Navy that they had to talk to a man whose name ended in a vowel. And so he picked up the nickname Jerry.

And so when I picked a nickname, I picked up Jerry, too. And I was pretty much a Jerry until I got on the Jefferson Airplane. And my ex-wife, Margareta, said, you know, you got a great name. Why don't you use it instead of Jerry? And I got to thinking about it. And I thought, that's a better rock 'n' roll name than Jerry. I'll take it.
BRIGER: Although, there's another Jerry on the scene, too (laughter).
KAUKONEN: Now, Mr. Garcia was certainly OK. Mr. Garcia was certainly OK with his name.
BRIGER: Well, I was wondering, you know, if you feel that some of those early experiences of being ostracized or being treated like an outsider sort of primed you for the counterculture when it came?
KAUKONEN: You know, I don't think I've ever thought about that before, before this conversation. But in a way, you're probably right. In a way, you're probably right.
BRIGER: If you're just joining us, our guest is singer, songwriter and guitarist Jorma Kaukonen of Jefferson Airplane and Hot Tuna. We'll be back after a short break. This is FRESH AIR.
BRIGER: This is FRESH AIR. We're talking with musician Jorma Kaukonen, best known as a founding member of Jefferson Airplane and Hot Tuna. He celebrated his 85th birthday last year.

So you said that when you were playing out when you were young, you would sometimes get criticized by other folkies because you weren't performing the songs exactly how they were recorded on the record.
BRIGER: And you said that authenticity was all about sounding just like somebody else.

KAUKONEN: Yeah. I think that - I don't think anybody would think about that today. That's a bygone thing. But to be - you know, in the in the social strata, whatever you want to call it, that I grew up, to be a folk singer was sort of like an outre kind of thing. And it was kind of a closed club in a lot of ways. And a lot of the people that played folk music, you know, we were all students of somebody else back in those days.

I mean, you know, Woody Guthrie, of course, was Woody Guthrie. But I didn't know Woody, you know? So we all kind of gravitated to whoever sort of inspired us to do things. And because of my inability to precisely replicate the people that I looked up to, like Reverend Gary Davis, for example, I just - I was just so excited about getting out there and doing it. And in the long run, you know, as an artist over the years, that certainly accrued to my benefit.
BRIGER: What's a song that you used to play a lot back then?
KAUKONEN: I play a lot of the same songs today. I would say "Candy Man Blues," for example.
BRIGER: Which is a Mississippi John Hurt song.
KAUKONEN: Yeah. Well, Reverend Davis - I'm going to slip these picks on while we're having this. I didn't learn the Mississippi version. The Reverend Davis version kind of goes
(Singing) Candy man been here and gone. Candy man been here and gone. Candy man been here and gone. Well, I wish I was in New Orleans sitting on a candy stand.

Yeah, et cetera, et cetera. And, yeah, it's a really cool song. And the reverend's version - I mean, there's so many versions of those to look at. But from a geeky guitar point of view, one of the things I think that got me about the reverend's version...
Instead of being a 5-4 bass is 5-3.
Kind of gives it a cool sound.
BRIGER: So you brought up Reverend Gary Davis here. He has been a huge influence on your musical life. You've recorded, like, a ton of his songs.
BRIGER: And he first gained notice, like, in the '30s, but then sort of was, quote, "rediscovered" in the '60s. So why do you think that he spoke so much to you?

KAUKONEN: You know, that's a really good question. And I remember David Bromberg and I had a discussion a couple of years ago about why so many young Jewish guitar players like David and myself gravitated towards Christian fundamentalist music. And that's a good question. And I don't have a ready answer for it.

But there was just something so complete about Reverend Davis' playing. I mean, he was just - well, for lack of a better word, he was just a monster. He had huge hands. He did all this incredibly complex contrapuntal stuff that if you didn't have hands that were that big is difficult if not impossible to do. And he was just incredibly inspiring. I mean, he was just always just like an upbeat. He was a biophile, a lover of life.
BRIGER: Yeah, and he actually was a reverend. It's not like he was, like, Professor Longhair. Like, he was a minister.
KAUKONEN: Yeah, right, right. He was.

BRIGER: And he would rarely - played, like, secular songs after a while. Or he'd play them, like, instrumental. And a lot of his songs he wrote were gospels, or he wrote religious songs. Yeah, so as you said, you weren't Christian. You weren't terribly religious then. Like, how did you...
BRIGER: How did you relate to those songs? Or did that just not matter?

KAUKONEN: Wow. It just really resonated with me on a primal level. And Reverend Davis, I got a chance to hang with him a little bit and see him play. At that time, he wasn't playing blues out. But when you got together with him and Mother Davis wasn't around, he'd play blues.
KAUKONEN: And sometimes some pretty raunchy blues, too. But...

KAUKONEN: ...Just - I mean, you have to realize that, as you mentioned, he really was a reverend, and I was very fortunate. He was a street singer. I got a chance to see him play on the street in Harlem. I mean, how cool is that?

BRIGER: You know, I always wondered about those blues singers from back then who were rediscovered in the '60s because, like, you know, when they were younger, they were usually poor. They lived their lives under Jim Crow and systemic racism.
BRIGER: Did you ever feel that they were skeptical of these, like, middle-class white kids that really wanted to learn their music?

KAUKONEN: You know, I never did. And that's not to say that that wasn't the case. It was just a conversation that I never had, you know, because over the years, I was fortunate enough and I got a chance to meet Reverend Davis a number of times. I think - I don't think that the disparity between the races and that - and the social consciousness of that time, I don't think that - it just didn't seem to, like, resonate with him in that kind of way. He just always seemed like an incredibly upbeat guy. And his life wasn't easy by any stretch the imagination. By the time that I met him, you know, thanks to, you know, the white, young blues culture at the time were starting to - you know, to make sure that he got a lot of gigs and stuff like that, but he just always just really seemed to be a lover of life. I think he just - I mean, who knows what he felt 'cause we don't get a chance to talk to him. But he just occupied a special place in all of our hearts for a lot of reasons. First of all, he was a musical genius, and secondly, he was a cool guy.
BRIGER: So you were at Santa Clara University in the Bay Area sometimes going to classes but mostly playing a lot of music and...
BRIGER: ...Performing at hootenannies. One of the people you met back then was Janis Joplin, who like you...
BRIGER: ...This was the pre-folk version of Janis Joplin and...
BRIGER: ...You two would play together. And even though she wasn't famous yet, you thought that there was something special there.

KAUKONEN: Yeah. They were - I remember, I guess it was probably the first week that I was in the South Bay area, and there was a flyer on campus that talked about a hootenanny in San Jose, and I figured, I'm there. And I went there, and a lot of people were hanging out there. Janis was there, and we got to talking, and she needed somebody to back her up, and we started messing around in this little dressing room that was the sound of - the size of a closet. And we wound up playing together and had a really good time.

So when Janis would come down the Peninsula to work a gig, I was the guy that she was - called because she didn't have to hire somebody from San Francisco. So I got to play with her a bunch of times. But I remember the first time I heard her, I thought, this is the real deal. This woman is a blues singer. And, you know, to be able to have accompanied her in that era was such an incredible honor, you know, in the way that things unfolded. Now, I'm not the only person who accompanied her, but, man, she was really something.
BRIGER: Well, there's a great archival recording of you and Janis playing together that's called the typewriter tape, and it...

BRIGER: ...Gets the name because of the improvised percussion your wife - or your wife-to-be at the time, Margareta, was doing, typing a letter to her parents. So I thought we would hear a little bit of "Hesitation Blues." This is a song that you would go on to play have played thousands of times in your life. It's another Reverend Gary Davis song. But let's hear a little bit of it.

JANIS JOPLIN: (Singing) Well, nickel is a nickel, dime is a dime. I need a new man, Lord, I know he won't mind. How long, Dear, do I have to wait? Can I get you now, Dear? Must I hesitate? Well, the eagle on the dollar says in God we trust. You say you want a baby, you want to see that dollar first. How long, Dear, do I have to wait? Can I get you now, Dear? Must I hesitate?
BRIGER: That's "Hesitation Blues" by Janis Joplin and my guest Jorma Kaukonen.
Jorma, let's take a short break here. We'll be right back after a moment. This is FRESH AIR.

And I figured, I'm going to need to go to Europe and be an expat American. And I thought I'd go to Copenhagen. I heard that Champion Jack Dupree was in Copenhagen. I thought maybe he'd let me play with him, et cetera. But I got sidetracked. I got sidetracked by Paul and the Jefferson Airplane. And, yeah, I mean, who knows if we'd be having this conversation today if Paul hadn't said, you know, I've moved to San Francisco, and we're messing around with a band. You might want to come up and take a listen.
BRIGER: So eventually you said yes.
KAUKONEN: I did. I was - you know, I was reluctant because it seemed so inauthentic at the moment, you know, to play rock 'n' roll. But, hey, I was a dumb kid. What did I know?

BRIGER: You actually gave the band its name, and it comes from a version of a blues name that you had at the time. JEFFERSON AIRPLANE: (Singing) One pill makes you larger, and one pill makes you small. And the ones that mother gives you don't do anything at all. Go ask Alice when she's 10 feet tall. And if you go chasing rabbits, and you know you're going to fall...

BRIGER: So those are two versions of "White Rabbit," the first by The Great Society, and then the second by Jefferson Airplane. So, you know, Jorma, those songs sound so different to me. Like, you added the Bolero beat. You have this haunting, like, guitar solo at the beginning. Like, do you remember how the version of that song came about for Jefferson Airplane?

KAUKONEN: Yeah, actually, I do. Yeah, so Grace brought that song. It was a great song. Anyway, so Jack came up with that little Bolero riff, and too bad we don't have him on the line with us to talk, but it's like, how do you come up with something like that? And the answer is, who knows? You have a...

And I think that - and I'm going to go with that because I can still play "Genesis" with the same intensity that I did when I wrote the song, (laughter) but I don't come away at the end of the song feeling miserable.
BRIGER: Now, that's what I was going to ask 'cause...
BRIGER: ...If you're a method actor, you might start to feel pretty terrible at that point.
KAUKONEN: Yeah, well, you got to know when to shut the method off.
BRIGER: Yeah. Well, you've said, I think I'm happier than some of the songs are, but I like the melancholy stuff. I like sniveling. I really do. Sometimes it just feels right to be miserable.
KAUKONEN: Yeah. Boy, though. That's a brilliant quote.
KAUKONEN: No, I said that. Yeah, I mean, I think I tend to gravitate towards emotional art than I do happy art. I don't know why. It just seems to be that way.

BRIGER: You know, one of the things I really liked about your memoir is that you talk about how you met your second wife, Vanessa, and how you really found love there. But, you know, you don't make it sound like a fairytale. Like, you keep it very honest. You know, you were still dealing with addictions at the time.
BRIGER: You fathered a son with another woman. But it seems like with Vanessa, like, you found a space that allowed you to make the changes that you needed to make in your life. Is that fair?

KAUKONEN: I think it's fair, and I think that it's safe to say that without Vanessa in my life, I may or may not have been here today, you know? We're an interesting partnership. It'd be fun if we had her in on this conversation, also, because I'm sure she looks at it a little differently than I do. But yeah, Vanessa was and is the love of my life.
BRIGER: If you're just joining us, our guest is singer, songwriter and guitarist Jorma Kaukonen of Jefferson Airplane and Hot Tuna. We'll be back after a short break. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF JORMA KAUKONEN SONG, "LATE IN THE EVENING")
BRIGER: This is FRESH AIR. We're talking with musician Jorma Kaukonen, best known as a founding member of Jefferson Airplane and Hot Tuna.

So in 2002, you released this album, "Blue Country Heart," with some really great Bluegrass musicians - Jerry Douglas on Dobro, Sam Bush on Mandolin, Béla Fleck is on a couple tunes on Banjo and the bass player Byron House. And you play a lot of songs of, like, the Delmore Brothers and Jimmie Rodgers. What was the impetus for this album?

KAUKONEN: What a fun project that was. First of all, look at the guys I got to play with. Secondly, there are no Franken-solos and stuff like that. That's all live. We cut that whole album live. And we never did more than two or three takes. It was exciting.
BRIGER: Well, maybe let's hear a little bit of your version of their song "Blue Railroad Train" from your album, "Blue Country Heart." Here it is.

KAUKONEN: (Singing) Blue railroad train going down the railroad track makes me feel so doggone blue listening to that old smokestack. Come back again, let me hear the whistle blow. Taking the sun and leaving the rain, and I hate to see you go.

BRIGER: That's my guest, Jorma Kaukonen, playing the Delmore Brothers song "Blue Railroad Train" from his 2002 album, "Blue Country Heart." You know, earlier we said that you find tranquility in the guitar. You're going to turn 86 this year, I think. Do you still find tranquility in it? Is it harder to play the guitar these days?

KAUKONEN: I do. I do still find tranquility in it. And it's difficult to - at this point in my life, it's difficult to still stumble on exciting turns in the road on the instrument because I've been doing it for so long, but not impossible 'cause I listen to a lot of different kind of music. And, you know, Vanessa will tell you, like, I'll just sit around the house with a guitar in my hand, not practicing, not even playing songs, but just, like, noodling in between conversations. I love the doggone thing.
BRIGER: Does your hand cramp up nowadays, or does it feel pretty supple?

KAUKONEN: I need to warm up in a way that I didn't when I was younger, and I'm very fortunate 'cause I don't have arthritis in my hands, but they're not as flexible as they used to, and I need to plan ahead with stuff. But again, I'm so blessed, physically, that I'm able to still play at a level that makes me want to keep on playing.
BRIGER: Before we go, is there a song that you've been playing recently that maybe means something different to you now that you just think about a lot that maybe you like to close with?

KAUKONEN: Oh, boy, let's see, that's a good question. Yeah. And I'm going to say "Trouble In Mind" simply because of the hook line, I won't be blue always. The sun's going to shine in my back door someday.
BRIGER: Would you mind playing a little bit of that?

(Singing) Trouble in mind. I'm blue. I won't be blue always because the sun gonna shine in my back door someday. Baby's gone. She's gone. She won't be going away because the sun gonna shine in my back door some day. Trouble in mind. I'm blue. I won't be going away because the sun gonna shine in my back door. I said the sun gonna shine in my back door. Well, the sun gonna shine in my back door someday.
BRIGER: Well, Jorma Kaukonen, thank you so much for coming to FRESH AIR.
KAUKONEN: Well, thanks for having me. It's been a pleasure.
GROSS: Jorma Kaukonen spoke with FRESH AIR's executive producer Sam Briger. Kaukonen's most recent album is called "Wabash Avenue." He's currently on tour.

Tomorrow on FRESH AIR, filmmaker Ava DuVernay returns to our show. She challenges the stories America tells about itself.
